items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's take a look at the integral

Content:
[MATH: I = \int_1^5\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x.]

Content:
Watch out! In this particular case, it is incorrect to say

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^5\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x \:{\color{red}\boldsymbol{=}}\: \ln|x-2| \,\Big|_1^5 = \ln 3 - \ln 1 = \ln 3.\quad{\color{red}\times}]

Content:
This is incorrect because the integrand [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x-2}] has an infinite discontinuity at [MATH: x=2,] and this point lies within the domain of integration! Therefore, we cannot directly apply the first fundamental theorem of calculus.

Content:
Instead, what we can do is write the original integral as a sum of improper integrals:

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^5\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x = \underbrace{\int_1^2\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x}_{I_1} + \underbrace{\int_2^5\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x}_{I_2}.]

Content:
Let's evaluate [MATH: I_1\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{1}^{2}(1)/(x − 2)dx|= lim_(a → 2^{−})∫_{1}^{a}(1)/(x − 2)dx; = lim_(a → 2^{−})\ln|x − 2||_{1}^{a}; = lim_(a → 2^{−})(\ln|a − 2|− \ln|1 − 2|); = lim_(a → 2^{−})(\ln|a − 2|− 0); = lim_(a → 2^{−})(\ln|a − 2|); = − ∞.]

Content:
Since [MATH: I_1] diverges, the integral [MATH: I] also diverges. Since we know that [MATH: I] diverges, there is no need to evaluate [MATH: I_2.]

Content:
In general, if a function [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: [a,b]] except at some point [MATH: c \in (a,b)] where it has an infinite discontinuity, then

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int_a^c f(x)\,\textrm d x + \int_c^b f(x)\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
The integral on the left-hand side is convergent if and only if both integrals on the right-hand side are convergent. If either integral on the right-hand side diverges, then the integral on the left-hand side also diverges.

sections.readable_text:
Given the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{e^{2x}}{1-e^{2x}},] which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 f(x) \,\textrm d x] is divergent
2. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^1 f(x) \,\textrm d x] is divergent
3. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^1 f(x) \,\textrm d x] is divergent

sections.normalized_html:
Let's evaluate each integral in turn.

  • Statement I is true. To compute the integral, we use the substitution [MATH: u = e^{2x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2\, \textrm d u = e^{2x}\,\textrm d x.] Calculating the integral, we get [MATH: ∫_{− 1}^{0}f(x)dx|= ∫_{− 1}^{0}(e^{2x})/(1 − e^{2x})dx; = (1)/(2)∫_{e^{− 2}}^{1}(1)/(1 − u)du; = − (1)/(2)lim_(a → 1^{−})[\ln|1 − u|]_{e^{− 2}}^{a}; = − (1)/(2)lim_(a → 1^{−})(\ln|1 − a|− \ln|1 − e^{− 2}|); = − (1)/(2)[− ∞ − \ln (1 − e^{− 2})]; = ∞.]

  • Statement II is true. To compute the integral in statement II, we use the same process as before. [MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}f(x)dx|= ∫_{0}^{1}(e^{2x})/(1 − e^{2x})dx; = (1)/(2)∫_{1}^{e^{2}}(1)/(1 − u)du; = − (1)/(2)lim_(a → 1^{+})[\ln|1 − u|]_{a}^{e^{2}}; = − (1)/(2)lim_(a → 1^{+})(\ln|1 − e^{2}|− \ln|1 − a|); = − (1)/(2)[\ln (e^{2} − 1) − (− ∞)]; = − ∞.]

  • Statement III is true. We can write down this integral by splitting it over the discontinuity at [MATH: x=0,] as follows: [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^1 f(x) \,\textrm d x = \displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 f(x) \,\textrm d x + \displaystyle \int_{0}^1 f(x) \,\textrm d x.] Since both integrals on the right-hand side are divergent, the integral on the left-hand side is divergent, too.

In conclusion, statements I, II, and III are all true.

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the denominator of the integrand vanishes at [MATH: x=1.] Therefore, to evaluate the integral, we need to split it up over the point of discontinuity: [MATH: ∫_{− 2}^{2}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx|= ∫_{− 2}^{1}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx_(⏟)_(I_{1}) + ∫_{1}^{2}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx_(⏟)_(I_{2})]

Let's evaluate the first integral. Using the substitution [MATH: u = x-1,] we get

[MATH: I_{1}|= ∫_{− 2}^{1}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx; = ∫_{− 3}^{0}(1)/(root(u, 3))du; = lim_(a → 0^{−})∫_{− 3}^{a}u^{− 1/3}du; = lim_(a → 0^{−})[(3)/(2)u^{2/3}]_{− 3}^{a}; = lim_(a → 0^{−})(3)/(2)[a^{2/3} − (− 3)^{2/3}]; = (3)/(2)[(0)^{2/3} − root((− 3)^{2}, 3)]; = − (3)/(2)root(9, 3).]

Similarly, for [MATH: I_2,] we have

[MATH: I_{2}|= ∫_{1}^{2}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx; = ∫_{0}^{1}(1)/(root(u, 3))du; = lim_(a → 0^{+})∫_{a}^{1}u^{− 1/3}du; = lim_(a → 0^{+})[(3)/(2)u^{2/3}]_{a}^{1}; = lim_(a → 0^{+})(3)/(2)[1^{2/3} − a^{2/3}]; = (3)/(2)[1 − 0]; = (3)/(2).]

Therefore, [MATH: ∫_{− 2}^{2}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx|= I_{1} + I_{2}; = − (3)/(2)root(9, 3) + (3)/(2); = (3)/(2)(1 − root(9, 3)).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's take a look at the integral

Content:
[MATH: I = \int_1^5\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x.]

Content:
Watch out! In this particular case, it is incorrect to say

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^5\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x \:{\color{red}\boldsymbol{=}}\: \ln|x-2| \,\Big|_1^5 = \ln 3 - \ln 1 = \ln 3.\quad{\color{red}\times}]

Content:
This is incorrect because the integrand [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x-2}] has an infinite discontinuity at [MATH: x=2,] and this point lies within the domain of integration! Therefore, we cannot directly apply the first fundamental theorem of calculus.

Content:
Instead, what we can do is write the original integral as a sum of improper integrals:

Content:
[MATH: \int_1^5\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x = \underbrace{\int_1^2\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x}_{I_1} + \underbrace{\int_2^5\dfrac 1 {x-2} \,\textrm {d}x}_{I_2}.]

Content:
Let's evaluate [MATH: I_1\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{1}^{2}(1)/(x − 2)dx|= lim_(a → 2^{−})∫_{1}^{a}(1)/(x − 2)dx; = lim_(a → 2^{−})\ln|x − 2||_{1}^{a}; = lim_(a → 2^{−})(\ln|a − 2|− \ln|1 − 2|); = lim_(a → 2^{−})(\ln|a − 2|− 0); = lim_(a → 2^{−})(\ln|a − 2|); = − ∞.]

Content:
Since [MATH: I_1] diverges, the integral [MATH: I] also diverges. Since we know that [MATH: I] diverges, there is no need to evaluate [MATH: I_2.]

Content:
In general, if a function [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: [a,b]] except at some point [MATH: c \in (a,b)] where it has an infinite discontinuity, then

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int_a^c f(x)\,\textrm d x + \int_c^b f(x)\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
The integral on the left-hand side is convergent if and only if both integrals on the right-hand side are convergent. If either integral on the right-hand side diverges, then the integral on the left-hand side also diverges.

Item 2 — Example: Identifying a Divergent Improper Integral With a Discontinuity at an Interior Point

Example Prompt:
Given the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{e^{2x}}{1-e^{2x}},] which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 f(x) \,\textrm d x] is divergent
2. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^1 f(x) \,\textrm d x] is divergent
3. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^1 f(x) \,\textrm d x] is divergent

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's evaluate each integral in turn.

- Statement I is true. To compute the integral, we use the substitution
[MATH: u = e^{2x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2\, \textrm d u = e^{2x}\,\textrm d x.]
Calculating the integral, we get
[MATH: ∫_{− 1}^{0}f(x)dx|= ∫_{− 1}^{0}(e^{2x})/(1 − e^{2x})dx; = (1)/(2)∫_{e^{− 2}}^{1}(1)/(1 − u)du; = − (1)/(2)lim_(a → 1^{−})[\ln|1 − u|]_{e^{− 2}}^{a}; = − (1)/(2)lim_(a → 1^{−})(\ln|1 − a|− \ln|1 − e^{− 2}|); = − (1)/(2)[− ∞ − \ln (1 − e^{− 2})]; = ∞.]

- Statement II is true. To compute the integral in statement II, we use the same process as before.
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}f(x)dx|= ∫_{0}^{1}(e^{2x})/(1 − e^{2x})dx; = (1)/(2)∫_{1}^{e^{2}}(1)/(1 − u)du; = − (1)/(2)lim_(a → 1^{+})[\ln|1 − u|]_{a}^{e^{2}}; = − (1)/(2)lim_(a → 1^{+})(\ln|1 − e^{2}|− \ln|1 − a|); = − (1)/(2)[\ln (e^{2} − 1) − (− ∞)]; = − ∞.]
- Statement III is true. We can write down this integral by splitting it over the discontinuity at [MATH: x=0,] as follows:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^1 f(x) \,\textrm d x = \displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 f(x) \,\textrm d x + \displaystyle \int_{0}^1 f(x) \,\textrm d x.]
Since both integrals on the right-hand side are divergent, the integral on the left-hand side is divergent, too.

In conclusion, statements I, II, and III are all true.

Item 5 — Example: Calculating an Improper Integral with a Discontinuity at an Interior Point

Example Prompt:
Find the value of [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-2}^2\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{x-1}}\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that the denominator of the integrand vanishes at [MATH: x=1.] Therefore, to evaluate the integral, we need to split it up over the point of discontinuity:
[MATH: ∫_{− 2}^{2}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx|= ∫_{− 2}^{1}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx_(⏟)_(I_{1}) + ∫_{1}^{2}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx_(⏟)_(I_{2})]

Let's evaluate the first integral. Using the substitution [MATH: u = x-1,] we get

[MATH: I_{1}|= ∫_{− 2}^{1}(1)/(root(x − 1, 3))dx; = ∫_{− 3}^{0}(1)/(root(u, 3))du; = lim_(a → 0^{−})∫_{− 3}^{a}u^{− 1/3}du; = lim_(a → 0^{−})[(3)/(2)u^{2/3}]_{− 3}^{a}; = lim_(a → 0^{−})(3)/(2)[a^{2/3} − (− 3)^{2/3}]; = (3)/(2)[(0)^{2/3} − root((− 3)^{2}, 3)]; = − (3)/(2)root(9, 3).]

Similarly, for [MATH: I_2,] we have
